name: Name
title: Part 2 Two: Prey for the Hunter

name: Name
body:
Old Korska was once the thriving capital of what was then the kingdom of Umbrey. Its wide stone streets were built for the hooves of the finest horses in the land, and its buildings of stone and timber were once marvels of engineering, architecture, and beauty. That was long ago, however, many years before Sorscha was even born.
By the time she was old enough to hear of it, Old Korska had long since fallen into ruin, a reminder of their history lost to the locals, a cautionary tale and bedtime story to anyone else in the Motherland. What had become the Volozk of Umbrey was an untamed land with few major cities. For centuries, since the founding of the Iron Kingdoms, the seat of power there had been Castle Tzepesci in the north, home to the last of the land’s former rulers, Vladimir Tzepesci, until his demise at Henge Hold.
It still was, so far as she knew, though no Tzepesci now inhabited it. The last she had heard it was held by Arloff Omirov, a man she knew and whom Vlad had trusted, leaving him behind as castellan until his child was old enough to take up the mantle. Now, however, she was told that Omirov was no longer at Castle Tzepesci, that he had been dismissed and replaced by an imperial lackey named Lysenko.

name: Name
body: This would have been shocking, infuriating news had she not learned so much in the last few hours that was far more shocking still. It had begun with the appearance of Bohdan Lesnoi, a man unlike any Sorscha had ever encountered. Vlad had often accused her of freezing her own heart, and she had to admit that, with the exception of her reaction to the Dark Prince himself, she had. This had protected her from a great many things over the years, and it, combined with her training and skill as a warcaster, had inured her to the presence of power. She had fought alongside some of the most potent arcanists in the world and against creatures and beings that could very nearly be called gods. From Lesnoi, she felt a power different than any she had ever encountered before. Charisma, it could easily have been called in another setting. Magnetism might have been more accurate. It wasn’t that she was attracted to him—he did not kindle in her any of the feelings that Vlad once had, feelings she had effectively choked to death in the years since he had left her. But Lesnoi put her at ease in a way that she—a soldier from the days of her youth—found disconcerting.

name: Name
body:
After only minutes of discourse, she found that she trusted this stranger far more than she should, and she had no doubt that others less insulated against his charms would gladly follow him to their deaths, should he require it.
"That man could sell ice in Uldenfrost," her mother used to say of particularly persuasive merchants hawking their wares in the marketplace. If the saying had ever been true of anyone, it was true of Bohdan Lesnoi.
After his unusual appearance, Lesnoi had calmed their initial hostilities by revealing that her missing soldiers were safe and fine; they had merely been spirited away. When she saw them again, they looked pale and shaken, but they were certainly unharmed. They spoke of the forest reshaping itself around their path, their own footprints disappearing behind them.
"You are a druid," Sorscha had said to Lesnoi, and it had been more accusation than question.
"You could call me that," he replied. "But I am quite unlike the blackclads with which you are familiar. Here, we are the children of Zevanna Agha. Many of us have known this land our entire lives. We keep to the old ways, honoring and living alongside the forest and those things that call it home. But we are not cannibals, and we do not worship the Devourer. Many amongst our number are more familiar with the religions of your cities in the west than the beliefs of the Circle Orboros."

name: Name
body:
"Your . . . number," Sorscha had said, again less a question than, this time, the implication of one.
"There are many who remember the old ways," Lesnoi replied. "In recent years, Zevanna Agha has called to us again, gathering us here to help defend our Motherland from a new threat—one which I think you know. Our numbers are not great when compared to the armies you have commanded, but nonetheless, we are many, and we are dedicated."
Lesnoi had shared these things as he led her and her troops deeper into the forests and the ruins of Old Korska. On the surface, the former capital looked not much different from how Sorscha had imagined it, based on the stories she had been told. The majority of the buildings had long since fallen into ruin, with trees a century or more old growing up through their foundations. The wide streets were cracked and, she imagined, would be choked with vegetation earlier in the year, though now the cold had driven all but the hardiest plants into hibernation, even if only a ghostly dusting of snow billowed here and there in the lonely wind that cut through the ruined capital.

name: Name
body:
Yet as they walked, she also saw evidence of life here. Among the ruined buildings were some that had been saved, repurposed, or rebuilt, while other structures had been constructed anew using old materials, helping them to blend in with their surroundings at a glance.
She saw soldiers passing to and from these buildings. Their armor bore little resemblance to even the ragged uniforms of the Winter Korps soldiers who followed her. Bedecked in furs, talons, fangs, and feathers, the armor these soldiers sported more closely resembled those she had seen among the Circle Orboros.
But she also saw them carrying heavy hunting rifles, and some of them still bore emblems, hats, or other decorations from prior service in what had then been the Winter Guard. "Though our warriors are different from those you are used to," Lesnoi explained as he led them through the ghostly city, "they are, to a one, fiercely loyal, and some, I see, are perhaps familiar to you. Many of us have been on this path since birth, but others have joined us more recently, often coming from the road you presently walk. Indeed, the core of our soldiers was drawn from the personal liegemen of Vlad Tzepesci himself."

name: Name
body:
The young prince, who had been looking around with wide eyes at all they passed, more impressed and less fearful than the soldiers who followed her, perked up at the mention of his father’s name, his avid eyes focusing on Lesnoi instead of the ruined city around them or the warriors they passed. Was it Sorscha’s imagination, or did the druid wink at the child, as if he already knew his secret—and, if he was, indeed, the Old Witch’s envoy, perhaps he did. However, the boy looked at Sorscha and didn’t say anything.
"Omirov?" Sorscha asked.
"He is here," Lesnoi replied. "You will meet him soon enough."
While some among their number preferred the sunlight of the surface and lived and worked in the repurposed buildings of the capital or in small villages hidden in the surrounding woods, Lesnoi explained, their might was consolidated beneath their feet.
"That is the real city," he said, "at least today."
For as long as Sorscha could remember, entry into the ruins of Old Korska had been forbidden by royal decree, and logging, hunting, and trapping were banned anywhere near it. The ostensible explanation was public safety. The ruins were said to be infested with bogrin, dregg, and possibly worse things—subterranean horrors left over from when the Orgoth wiped the city from the map. Not to mention that the crumbling ruins themselves could be dangerous.

name: Name
body:
Now, however, Sorscha wondered if that had ever been true.
"As you saw," Lesnoi said, "the ways in and out of the city are hidden, guarded. Our underground sanctuary is even more so. I doubt that any of you could find your way back here again, but even so, I trust you will understand that additional precautions must be taken."
He produced a handful of strips of reddish fabric from a pouch. "Your soldiers can remove them when we are underground," he said.

name: Name
body: Sorscha counted the blindfolds in her hand before handing them to Sergeant Agrinov. He looked at her uncertainly, and she nodded. She saw him gulp before sheepishly passing them out to the other soldiers. "You’re two short," Sorscha said to Lesnoi. "Zevanna Agha says that we can trust you and the young . . . man," Lesnoi replied, his pause just long enough to convey silently to Sorscha that he was, indeed, aware of the prince’s identity and of her attempts to conceal it. "Her faith in you is enough for us." Sorscha shook her head. "For now, at least, these soldiers and this boy are under my command," she said. "As they go, so go I." For a moment, Lesnoi looked at her appraisingly, then he nodded and handed her two more blindfolds. She helped the kid fasten his around his eyes before she put on her own. He looked disappointed, but he went along without a fuss. The result of the blindfold wasn’t total darkness. Light still penetrated at the edges of the thick fabric. But it was effectively complete blindness, and though she knew that she could remove it in a moment, the sensation was disquieting. Though she was so accustomed to wearing warcaster armor that she hardly noticed it anymore, her boiler did produce an uncomfortable heat, even in the cold of Khadoran winter. A heat that made sweat gather along her back, and across her chest. As she tied the blindfold over her eyes, that sweat turned cold, and she hoped that her palms were not clammy with it when the kid slid his hand into hers.

name: Name
body: Of course, she could also see what was going on around her simply by switching her awareness to Bear’s, seeing what the warjack saw. For now, though, she didn’t. The blindfold was about the morale of her troops. Especially in this unfamiliar situation, she needed them to trust her, and for that, they needed to feel like she was one of them. And after so much time checked out from the world, maybe she needed to feel it, too. "Stay close," she said to the soldiers under her command, "and stay alert, but nobody take any action unless I give the order. Is that understood?" Murmurs of assent were enough, and then Lesnoi was leading them again, their steps guided unerringly by the almost melodic sound of his voice. "As I said," the Umbrean’s words ushered them along, "our army is not as large as those you’re used to, but it is growing. For years now, the Children of Agha have waited in the shadows, knowing that there would come a time when we were needed. More than once, we have mustered our forces, believing the time had arrived, only to be stopped by a restraining hand from our spiritual Mother. We have waited and prepared for the day when the Motherland called out to us. Now that day has arrived, and we are here to heed the call."

name: Name
body:
Sorscha and her troops followed his voice. For a time, they walked in sunlight that she could see at the edges of the blindfold, but before long, the light grew dimmer, amber-colored. They were descending, she knew, not by steps, but along some kind of enormous earthen ramp, one that could probably have carried wagons and certainly was large enough that Bear had no trouble finding footing upon it.
"You can take off your blindfolds now," Lesnoi said after the path under their feet had leveled off. Before doing so, Sorscha flicked her awareness to Bear’s, so that any surprise she felt wouldn’t show on her face when she pulled her blindfold down.
Korska had been a modern city before the devastation by the Orgoth. Its undercity had included miles of sewers, cellars, burial chambers, catacombs, and more. In the years—how many?—that the so-called "children" of the Old Witch had been here, they had carved these out, connected them. Lesnoi had called this the "real city," and he wasn’t exaggerating.

name: Name
body:
The place where he had led them looked like a market square, but no one was peddling wares. Instead, it was bustling as men, women, and children worked side-by-side grinding meal, tanning hides, cooking food on spits ventilated with carefully placed flues leading up to the outside air, and more. It looked for all the world like what it was—a military encampment, yes, but also home for dozens, if not hundreds, of families.
"Welcome," Lesnoi said, "to Umbrey."
***
"Sorscha," a familiar voice said from over her shoulder. "Sorscha Kratikoff. I won’t say you’re the last person I expected to see here, but you certainly aren’t the first."
It had been years since Sorscha had last seen Arloff Omirov, but she recognized him immediately. His black hair was cut short, his eyes the gray of gunmetal. And unlike most of the men she had seen underground, he was clean-shaven. He still looked like the soldier he had been the last time she saw him, even if his clothes no longer quite fit the picture.
He was dressed like most of the other warriors—it felt odd to call them soldiers—she had seen since her arrival in Korska, though an old Winter Guard greatcoat was draped over his shoulders rather than furs or a cloak. A rifle was slung over his shoulder, a sword at his hip. His smile was warm and genuine.

name: Name
body: Sorscha allowed herself to be pulled into a hug, and when she stepped back, Omirov looked her up and down appraisingly. "What brings you here?" he asked. "The machinations of an old woman," Sorscha replied, shaking her head. "And more than that. What brings you here?" "Things have changed since you’ve been away. The empire is different from the one I knew. I’m not saying it’s worse—or better—but I no longer know my place in it. The Motherland, though, remains as she always has, and she still needs us. I swore an oath to Vlad Tzepesci before he left that I would safeguard this land. And these people," Omirov swept out his hand to indicate the network of subterranean tunnels around them, "are the best way I can think to do that." "You knew my—" the boy began, then looked quickly at Sorscha. "You knew Vlad Tzepesci?" "Kid," Sorscha said, "this is Arloff Omirov. He knew Vlad Tzepesci better than probably anyone alive. Arloff, this is Tobias." She leaned forward, however, and whispered to Omirov who the boy really was, information that she was keeping it quiet for now. His gray eyes widened slightly, but he mastered his expression admirably.

name: Name
body:
"It’s a pleasure to meet you, son," he said, squatting down so that he was closer to the child’s height and taking the boy’s hand to shake.
"Can you tell me about him?" the boy asked.
Omirov cast a glance at Sorscha. A tiny smile touched the corners of her mouth, and she nodded. "I’ll have work to do here, I think," she said, "and I can’t imagine better hands that I could leave him in in the meantime."
***
The black horse beneath him was itself an accursed abomination, blighted by the terrible magic unleashed by the Orgoth. Its eyes should have been blind beneath the metal grill that covered them, and where wounds marred its sides, a sickly green light oozed forth. Yet it carried his massive weight with ease, its hooves chewing up the miles that separated him from his prey, and unlike other animals, it did not balk at the presence of the fell axe chained to his right hand.
Orsus had never named the horse, which had been brought to him by Sabbreth, and she hadn’t told him a name for the animal. On its back, he rode at the head of a small but terrible force, one chosen for its speed, to strike quickly and leave nothing alive.

name: Name
body:
Nearest behind him were two Jackals—fast and deadly warjacks of the strange design that the Orgoth had brought back to Immoren with them. Orsus had found that he could, with a little guidance, control these as easily as he had once controlled the warjacks of his homeland. Slightly behind them came the heavier tread of a Tyrant.
These were followed by the few troops that Orsus had chosen to accompany him. They traveled on foot but, unlike the Winter Guard he had commanded in his past life, they did not reluctantly trudge toward conflict; they seemed barely able to constrain themselves from sprinting to their next battle. At the front were the ulkors—massive cannibals with red-hued flesh that reminded Orsus of the ogrun he had sometimes been compared to. Behind them came Orgoth reavers armed with hand weapons and bolt throwers. They traveled  in the shadows of the half-dozen vulture-like rhoks that glided overhead.
Since encountering the Orgoth on that bloody beach, Orsus had enjoyed an odd clarity. His memory of his past was nothing but ghosts and shadows, but he knew that he had spent much of his life uncertain, searching for something that even he couldn’t name. Had he found it here? He couldn’t say, but for the first time in his life, he felt like he was only in the moment that he now occupied, not in a past that was a gaping pit, not in a future that was a red haze. Only this moment, as the horse ran beneath him, its hooves kicking up clods of frozen dirt, and the nightmares of an entire continent ran at his back.

name: Name
body: Even in the depths of his madness, Orsus had been a natural tactician. He had always known where to stand to avoid being seen, how to move to flush his prey into a kill box. He had been trained, like all warcasters, but he had risen through the ranks with surprising speed, and even his teachers had been shocked by his ability to maneuver troops unerringly in the wargames that were played at the Druzhina. Commanding the Orgoth had required some adjustments but surprisingly few. Indeed, if anything, commanding the troops that followed him now came more naturally to him than leading the Winter Guard ever had. These warriors echoed his own blood thirst, and they were fanatics, willing to die without question if he gave the order, accustomed to the idea that they might be put to death for failure. They would not hesitate at any order. Without a thought, they would butcher women and children. With only a little more hesitation, they would die themselves. In many ways, they were more like the warjacks had always been. Less men and women than extensions of his own will. A weapon in his hand and, like any weapon in his hand, they hungered to spill blood. As the horse beneath him rode on and on toward Old Korska, he knew that it wouldn’t be long now.

name: Name
body: "They are drawing close now," Bohdan Lesnoi said, "your enemies and mine. The birds tell me of their coming." "Your tricks with the woods?" He shook his head. "The man who rides at the head of them—you know him, I think—he is cursed. That curse will cut through our defenses like a hot blade through tallow. We will have to fight them here." "I never wanted to not fight them," Sorscha said with a grim smile. "It was always just a matter of when and where." "You, your soldiers . . . you will see things in this fight. Things no outsider has ever seen. Are they prepared? Are you?" "Probably not," Sorscha replied, "but it seems we don’t have much choice. I don’t know what’s going on here, not really, but I know what’s coming, and I know that it has to be stopped." "Good enough," Lesnoi said. "See that your troops understand. The battle will come soon." *** Sorscha was accustomed to thinking of armies in terms of columns and formations, but the Orgoth didn’t move like that. Not that they were disorganized—they came on like a natural disaster, like a forest fire sweeping across the land. Before she could see them, she saw the animals that came ahead of them. Birds first, Lesnoi’s crows and others, darkening the sky, then smaller prey animals, rabbits, and even deer rushing past to escape what was coming.

name: Name
body:
They were waiting to meet the Orgoth force outside Old Korska. Bhodan Lesnoi had chosen the spot, a place where a shallow natural valley gave Sorscha’s troops high ground and forced the enemy to bunch together. Sorscha had requested certain changes to the landscape—piles of brush and other obstructions to funnel the Orgoth forces into overlapping fields of fire where her few soldiers could make the best of their limited resources. The Butcher would know it for the trap it was, would spot it immediately, but that didn’t necessarily mean he wouldn’t still drive his troops into it.
A small stream meandered through the vale, its waters clear, cold, and shallow enough for anyone to easily wade across. Sorscha and Bear had taken up a position on a hillock overlooking the battlefield, and her troops were arrayed on either side of her. Bear wasn’t much good in a firefight, but he could act as a shield, and they’d be happy to have the warjack when the enemy closed the distance between them.
Of course, Sorscha and her ragtag handful of troops were merely the bait. She knew it, and so did they. Bohdan Lesnoi had explained the battle plan to her, and she had explained it to them. How they were to lure the Orgoth into place so that the Umbrean forces could close around them like the talons of a hunting bird.

name: Name
body: "You must not be surprised by anything you see," Lesnoi had told her again. "We’re about to fight this continent’s oldest nightmare," she had replied. "I don’t think you need to worry." Now, though, standing on that cold hill, watching her breath steam in the air and waiting for the first sight of the enemy, she was worried. How had she gotten here, so far from what passed for home, allied with strangers and, possibly, with monsters, against a threat that had been little more than a storybook bogeyman since before she was born? As a girl, she had imagined the Orgoth as blood-soaked giants. She remembered the occasional girlhood nightmare of black carapaces, like enormous insects, corpses impaled upon their many spines. As a soldier, she had seen enough to know better. She had seen the leftovers of the Orgoth empire and had seen what they could do to her fellow soldiers. She had seen the prisoners chained to the screaming blades recovered from Orgoth tombs, their minds eroded by the gibbering voices of the dead. She had seen Orgoth secrets pulled from ancient graves by the necromancers of the Nightmare Empire and the Greylords of her own country, had seen the twisted abominations that issued forth as a result.

name: Name
body:
She knew that the Orgoth had been just men—in some ways, no different than those who shivered in the cold at her side. In other ways, however, they may as well have been the insectile horrors of her childhood nightmares. The culture of the Orgoth, what could be extracted from the stories of those who survived their reign and the few relics they left behind, portrayed a life utterly alien to her own. As such, she had no idea what to expect when they arrived in the valley, and a part of her anticipated the serrated shadow shapes of her childhood imagination.
What first rode into view, however, was a sight considerably more familiar. She had never seen Orsus Zoktavir on a horse before, and she felt sorry for the poor creature that had to carry his considerable bulk, but she recognized him easily, instantly, even from across the valley. The armor he wore was unfamiliar—sharp and alien, glowing with an amber illumination—and the axe chained to his right wrist was nearly as large as he was. But that it was Orsus Zoktavir, there was no doubt.

name: Name
body: Behind him came what could only be warjacks. Like Zoktavir’s armor, they glowed an angry amber, and even the smallest of them were wide-shouldered brutes with the gait of a gorax, their backs bristling with blades, their arms with unfamiliar weapons. The larger reminded her of a heavy Cryxian ’jack, its tusked head and massive, crushing claw visible even from this distance. Soldiers followed, hulking, ogrun-like figures with axes in either hand, smaller troops wearing the black armor of the Orgoth. With nothing more than a raise of his left fist, Zoktavir brought them up short at the edge of the valley. And despite their bestial appearance, they stopped with an uncanny discipline. The Butcher of Khardov examined the valley, his gaze traveling across Sorscha’s meager troops, and she could tell he was smiling. He sees the trap, she thought. But that hadn’t ever been a question. The question was: Would he still take it? Sorscha could feel her heart beating, the rush of blood in her veins. To her ears, it sounded painfully loud as she waited. For several long moments, the Butcher eyed the terrain between them, the Orgoth forces panting around him. Then, he pulled an ivory-colored horn from his belt and blew into it—a single, mournful note that seemed to hang in the still air—and his soldiers began to pour into the valley.

name: Name
body:
There were not many, yet they seemed to fill the space in a heartbeat, black armor and flashing blades surging toward the hillock where she stood. To either side, her soldiers were fanned out in a single line, rifles at the ready, but they held . . . held . . . the note of the horn still echoing around them.
"Fire!" Sorscha shouted, and as the air was filled with the crack of rifles, the trees around the valley seemed to come alive with monsters.
***
Orsus knew an ambush when he saw one. The woman on the other side of the shallow swale, with her dark hair and sharp eyes, was familiar. He had known her in another life and knew she was a soldier of great talent and intelligence. She would not have faced him like this, in the open and with so few ragged soldiers at her side, if it were anything but a trap.
Still, he could not detect its mechanism. Such things had always come easily to him, as naturally as breathing, yet now his eyes scanned the trees in search of soldiers and found none, skimmed the open ground between his force and hers for hidden earthworks but couldn’t see any. Whatever she had planned, he couldn’t divine its means, and that intrigued him. Had it been otherwise, perhaps he would have shown more caution, sent scouts ahead, fanned his troops to avoid a flanking maneuver. But the very obviousness of the trap, combined with its seeming invisibility, piqued his curiosity and made him want to see it sprung.

name: Name
body:
And yet he did not forget his mission. In a short time, he had learned the ways of the Orgoth. His soldiers were expendable, every last one of them. If he returned alone, bloodied, without a single survivor under his command, he would still be the victor so long as he had accomplished his mission. This was how the Orgoth thought, how the Orgoth lived. It was part of what made them so dangerous, so terrible. It was part of what made him one of them.
So, he sent his soldiers into the trap ahead of him, though he would have preferred to be at the front of the tide of blood that was coming. He had to personally delay and watch. This was not the mission. This was merely entertainment.
Even from here, he could feel the terror that poured off the handful of soldiers arrayed on the opposite side of the valley. He could all but see their pale, sweaty skin, their fingers shaking against the triggers of their rifles as they awaited the order to fire. They knew that they were the bait in a trap, and though they hoped to see it close before they died, they knew also that not all of them would survive it.

name: Name
body:
Orsus knew Khadoran military rifles, knew that the bolt throwers carried by the reavers under his command had greater range. But he also knew that the ulkors would run ahead, so the Winter Korps would fire before his troops did. As the crack of the rifles echoed through the still air, the trap was sprung, and Orsus saw something unexpected.
He was a child again, huddled in the cellar of his family’s small home. He could hear the sound of rats in the darkness, but his fear of them was nothing compared to his fear of the silence from above. He had to stay quiet and protect his mother and sister, who crouched with him in the darkness. His father had stayed behind to protect them. Orsus had begged to join him. "I’m big," he had told his father, "I can fight!"
"I need you to live," his father had told him, "and to take care of your mother and sister." That had been the mission, then, as the cellar door opened and the Tharn pulled him up and into a nightmare.
His father was dead, a puddle of blood and broken bones on the floor, and his house was on fire, the air full of embers that burned as they struck his skin. And that was only the beginning. Amid it all stood a bad dream, a bogeyman, its body knotted sinew, its face terribly human, though surrounded by a mane of thick fur.

name: Name
body:
"I can fight," he had said, but he couldn’t. He stood in frozen terror as the monster plunged a dagger of bone into his stomach, and he knew that he was dead. Yet he hadn’t died. Instead, a red mist had settled over him for the first time, and he had slain his killer with its own dagger, slitting its throat and feeling its hot blood rushing out.
Orsus didn’t know if the memory was real or part of his madness. A voice from the axe or a voice from his past. It didn’t matter. It was over now, gone, and he was again in the small valley, watching as new horrors poured from the woods around him. Things reminiscent of that Tharn and yet wildly different.
The crows were first. Great clouds of them seemed to materialize from the trees, striking at the rhoks where they wheeled through the sky, led by one unnaturally massive bird, its head the red of dried blood. Next came beasts, bigger than any wolves Orsus had ever seen, nightmare conglomerations of bone and fur, teeth and talons and horns, pouncing from the shadows to plow into the flank of the reavers, teeth sinking through black armor as one Orgoth was hauled from his feet and hurled into the air like a child’s doll.

name: Name
body:
That wasn’t the end. Something else was coming from the trees. Something bigger. So, that was the trap, the secret. His enemy had allied themselves with the druids, with cannibals and monsters. He supposed he had, too. It didn’t matter. None of it did. All those years ago, amid fire and the smell of blood, he had killed one monster from the woods. Now, he would kill these, too.
***

name: Name
body:
There had been a terrible, lurching moment when Sorscha thought that Bohdan Lesnoi had abandoned them. When it seemed as if she could almost feel the hot breath of the enemy, just before the rifles began their reports all around her, the bullets piercing flesh but not even slowing the onrushing enemy down.
Then the darkness came, a shadow blotting out the thin winter sun as crows rose from the trees around them. And as the resulting shadows seemed to come alive, she realized why she hadn’t seen Lesnoi’s troops take their positions. He hadn’t brought liegemen to fight this battle—he had brought monsters.
Loping predators as big as horses, their bodies a chimeric witch’s brew of different beasts. Something bigger, like a warjack, but terribly alive, its head a leering, horned skull from which hungry eyes glowed. They would probably have turned her blood cold in any other context. Now, as they seemed to materialize out of the trees and fall upon the Orgoth, they were as welcome as old friends—not that she had long to appreciate that thought before the enemy reached her ragged line.

name: Name
body:
The ogrun-like hulks were first, axes in each hand, and they expected to cut a bloody swath through the shaky infantry Sorscha had arranged, but they never got the chance. She had been holding onto Bear’s metaphorical leash for just this moment, and now she let it go, the massive warjack surging in front of her and plowing into the enemy—the proverbial rock and a hard place.
Axes clanged against iron as Bear’s massive fists fell among the enemy, and Sorscha felt hot blood spatter her face and freeze there, even as she gathered her magic.
The confusion of the springing trap didn’t last. What had appeared to be a chaotic, unruly charge suddenly formed ranks, the Orgoth soldiers locking their shields together to fire wickedly barbed bolts from unfamiliar weapons. One caught Pachek in the throat. He pitched to the snowy ground with a gurgling cry and didn’t move, a red stain spreading from him. Others tore into the horrors that had emerged from the dark woods.
Around her, the rifles cracked again, but she couldn’t focus on any of it. One of the axers had gotten past Bear. Its left arm was broken, hanging useless at its side, but in its right hand it still held a gleaming axe that was swinging for her face. She could have blocked, but she didn’t, allowing the blade instead to skip off the power field of her warcaster armor while she gathered the cold around her into herself, feeling it well up inside as the icy runes appeared around her wrists. For the first time, she saw something that might have been fear on the face of the brutish Orgoth as she extended her hand, and a sharp, cold wind took shape, slicing her foe to bloody ribbons that froze before they reached the ground.

name: Name
body:
Against another force, the attack might have been a rout, the combined surprise and terror of Lesnoi’s monstrous allies enough to splinter the resolve of a common soldier in a tide of blood and talons, fur and teeth. But the Orgoth were far from ordinary, and the initial chaos of the encounter was past—the remaining Orgoth soldiers formed a hard knot of armor and weapons, the beasts of the woods breaking around them like water flowing past a rock. Moreover, Lesnoi had shown himself now, his flowing robes coalescing from a flock of crows at the valley's edge—and Zoktavir had seen him.
The Butcher had stayed uncharacteristically aloof from the melee, waiting at the valley's far side with three unfamiliar warjacks in tow. The Butcher, who now raised that long, curved horn to his lips once more, and blew a terrible, wavering note, one that seemed to scrape across Sorscha’s brain. As the chill note reverberated in her bones, she saw something that froze her blood. The fallen Orgoth were picking themselves up.

name: Name
body:
These were not dazed or battered soldiers being rallied for a fresh attack. These were the dead, now dead no more. Here, a soldier with a bullet hole through his face large enough that she could have put her fist through it, there one whose arm had been rent so far from his body that it simply hung on a bloody spit of bone. Even the bloody, frozen remnants of the beast at her feet began to knit themselves together as she watched.
Whatever advantage their ambush had granted them was undone in a moment by a single blast from the Butcher’s accursed horn, and Sorscha felt her resolve draining, her grip on Frostfang loosening. Even as she faltered, the Butcher smiled and dug his heels into the flanks of the massive black horse, charging onto the field.
***
When the lady left him, she had knelt in front of him first. "I need you to stay with Omirov," she said, putting her hand awkwardly on his shoulder. "He knows what’s going on. He’ll take care of you. You can trust him."
"Will you come back?" he had asked.

name: Name
body:
"That’s the plan," she’d replied, but he didn’t believe her.
For a time, Omirov, who insisted that young Vlad call him Arloff, had told him stories about his father. These weren’t like the ones the lady told him. These were more like those he had already heard at the palace, tales of his father’s victories in battle, of his heroism, his valor, though Omirov told them with warmth and a familiarity that could only have come from actually being there to witness them himself.
The underground city was busy, however, and Omirov faced constant interruptions that dragged his attention away from Vlad, who nonetheless followed obediently along. Besides the soldiers who were coming and going, looking more like hunters than the soldiers he watched drilling at the palace, there were other kids, some near his own age.
Vlad was accustomed to being watched. Indeed, he rarely had more than a moment or two alone in the course of his day. This also meant that he had learned how to make time for himself, even when he was supposed to be elsewhere. He had slipped off in the palace more than once, only for his governess or tutor to later find him watching the mechaniks working on the warjacks.

name: Name
body:
He waited until Omirov was distracted, and he switched coats with one of the boys his own age, promising the other child that he could keep the much nicer greatcoat, with its shiny buttons, so long as he would trail along behind Omirov for a while in Vlad’s place.
Now wrapped in a fur that smelled like woodsmoke, Vlad slipped away even as the other boy took up his position at Omirov’s side while the soldiers discussed plans to reinforce the city in case the attackers broke through.
Vlad was unclear on precisely what was happening, but from the moment the old woman appeared in his bedroom, he knew one thing—it was because of him. "Out there, it doesn’t matter who your father is," the lady told him, but he knew it did. Maybe it shouldn’t, but it did.
Somewhere not far away, the lady and the handful of soldiers—the one who had helped him up when he fell in the snow, the one who had shared her rations, the one who had showed him how to open the boiler on the warjack—were fighting a battle against a terrible enemy, one that he didn’t understand, couldn’t even imagine. One that, though she hid it well, the lady was afraid of. And he knew that the only reason the enemy was here—the only reason any of them were here—was because of him.

name: Name
body: The old woman had taken him from his room in the palace and brought him here to keep him away from them. Now, the lady and the soldiers were fighting and maybe dying to keep him safe. As the heir apparent to the Khadoran Empire, he had been raised to expect people to fight and die for him. His mother gave daily orders that shaped the lives of countless thousands of people—and sometimes ended them. But that, he somehow knew, was different. He didn’t want these people to die because of him, not while he was hiding underground. Something else the lady had said echoed in his memory. "Your father was a great man, it’s true. But he was great because of what he did and who he was, not because of how he was born. And however you turn out, great or disappointing, will be because of what you do, not because of who your father was." His father had sacrificed himself for the Motherland, for all of Immoren. Vlad knew that. It was practically the first thing about his father he had ever learned. He didn’t think he wanted to sacrifice himself, necessarily, but he didn’t want the lady or the soldiers to sacrifice themselves in his place, either. Wherever they were, whatever was happening, it was tied to his destiny—and he would go to meet it.

name: Name
body:
"Fall back," Sorscha shouted to Sergeant Agrinov. "Get those things between you and the enemy."
The sight of the Butcher joining the fray had shaken her from her stupor, had reminded her of why she was here. It had lit a fire in her again. When everything else was gone, she still had her hatred of Orsus Zoktavir, and if she were going to die in this valley, it was going to be while spitting her blood in his face.
"What about you?" Sergeant Agrinov asked, once again forgetting his decorum.
"I have places to be."
The Butcher wasn’t charging toward her, and he wasn’t coming to reinforce his troops, who were now fully locked into place in the middle of the valley, surrounded by monsters. He was riding straight toward Bohdan Lesnoi, who stood seemingly unprotected at the edge of the woods.
Whenever Sorscha used her magic, she could feel its cold. First in her lungs, then spreading outward to her fingertips. Now, she forced energy into Bear to speed his step so he could accompany her as she crossed the battlefield to where the Butcher was already closing on his prey.

name: Name
body:
The two smaller warjacks that followed the Butcher were faster than the heavy that trailed behind. As she sprinted across the field, dodging the heaving bodies of the chimeric beasts from the woods, the nearest one pivoted slightly and opened fire on her, flinging heavy bolts that whined through the air.
She ducked one, her boots sliding in the snow beneath her, while the other struck Bear in the shoulder—a glancing blow, no significant damage. The ’jack moved to interpose itself between her and her target, however, even as the Butcher galloped on toward Lesnoi.
Sorscha slowed, allowing caution to temper her actions as Bear moved ahead of her like a freight train. The next bolt from the ’jack buried itself in Bear’s face but thankfully missed its optics. The enemy warjack’s other hand clutched an ornate mace, which it brought around to meet Bear’s charge but not quite fast enough.
Bear plowed into the smaller ’jack, sending it sprawling. Without pause, it began hammering at the fallen enemy with its armored fists, and Sorscha was relieved to see scraps of black metal flying from the melee.

name: Name
body:
Unfortunately, this attracted the attention of the bigger Orgoth warjack, and it fired not at Bear but at Sorscha herself, a red-hot blast that exploded against her power field, the flash briefly blinding her and knocking her back into the snow. The monstrous ’jack was only a few yards away, closing on her as Bear abandoned its downed prey to meet this new attacker.
The Orgoth heavy chopped into Bear with its massive claw, ripping the Kodiak’s left arm free of its socket in a spray of torn metal. Sorscha felt the injury herself, a phantom pain that shot through her arm and left her fingertips tingling in its wake. Bear didn’t slow down, though, bringing its remaining fist around and into the side of the other ’jack’s head.
The Butcher reined in his horse, but the other light ’jack continued its forward momentum. This one’s right arm held a long-handled weapon that it swept at Lesnoi, only to find thin air where he had previously been as he dissolved into a flock of crows. The warjack wasn’t to be disappointed for long, however, as something came barreling out of the woods like a cannonball, striking the ’jack with enough force to send it stumbling even as it was enwrapped in dark, leathery wings.

name: Name
body:
Sorscha had once captured a wounded bat when she was a girl, though her mother had warned her not to pick it up, as its bite might carry disease. The way this thing moved reminded her of that fierce little animal, but it was much, much bigger, and as a gap appeared in its leathery wings, she saw that its head was that of an antlered owl, its beak rending the metal of the smaller ’jack.
Everything around her seemed to slow. Bear’s dismembered arm crashing to the ground in a spray of soot-stained snow. The sound of the battle everywhere around her dropping away, her vision tunneling as she locked eyes with the Butcher of Khardov, the man who had killed her father.
For years, she had dreamed of killing him. Even when she had fought side-by-side with this man, commanding the armies of the Motherland, she had buttressed herself with visions of him choking on his own blood as she carved out his throat. Now, at last, they were about to meet on the battlefield.
Orsus Zoktavir wheeled his horse and smiled, and Sorscha knew she had walked into a trap, as surely as he had. Like him, however, there was no place she would rather be.

name: Name
body:
The Butcher didn’t even have to dig his heels into the horse’s flank. It was as if horse and rider were one as the massive black animal began a galloping charge toward where Sorscha lay in the snow, Zoktavir hoisting that warjack-sized axe above his head as he came.
***
Vlad stood at the edge of the trees and looked out at something from one of the scary stories his governess sometimes told him. There were monsters everywhere. A huge, shaggy beast with a skull for a head drove a spear into a humanoid figure in black armor. Things like wolves or bears but bigger than any Vlad had ever seen, even in the zoo in Korsk, stalked among soldiers who fired unfamiliar weapons. There were even machines like warjacks yet alien, slimmer and stranger than any he had ever seen.
Amid all of this, however, he saw the familiar red coats of the soldiers he had arrived here with. They were fewer in number now, and they clustered on a nearby hill, firing desperately at the melee that surrounded them. He also saw the lady, her own red coat wet with melted snow and smeared with mud, as a huge man, maybe the biggest man Vlad had ever seen, swung an axe so large that it should have been impossible for him to lift it.

name: Name
body:
The enormous axe crashed against the lady’s weapon. Vlad had been taught a little about how warcaster armor worked, and he saw the crackle of her power field as it shook and then failed under the tremendous blow, which pushed her backward, digging her boots into the snow.
He saw her switch her grip on the strange weapon she carried, freeing up her left hand. Runes began to gather around it, as he knew happened when a warcaster was going to cast a spell—and then he saw the runes die away without effect. The big man smiled cruelly and said something, though Vlad was too far away to hear what it was.
The lady barely parried the next blow of the axe. The clang echoed even over the din of the rest of the battle, and her boots dug not just into snow but into the frozen ground beneath. Vlad could tell that the battle had been going on for a while. There were dead bodies on the ground. The warjack the lady secretly called Bear, and he pretended he didn’t know the name of, was missing an arm as it fought a weakening skirmish against one of the unfamiliar ’jacks.

name: Name
body:
The big man bore several fresh wounds, Vlad could see, including one across his cheek, while the lady spat a red glob of blood onto the snow as she wheeled, stepping to the side and swinging Frostfang around into a graceful blow that the big man somehow blocked with the flat of his axe. Now Vlad could see that the axe was covered in faces. At first, he thought they were just carvings, but as he watched, he saw that they moved and screamed.
Lashing out with his other arm, the big man struck Kommander Kratikoff across the face with a horn he carried. She stumbled, and he kicked her knee, her leg folding up beneath her as she went down in the snow before him. Her power field was clearly depleted, and blood drooled from her mouth as she looked up at the massive axe, waiting for it to fall.
***
The battle had been as short as it was brutal. Sorscha was on her feet by the time the Butcher reached her, and she stepped nimbly aside from his first charge, Frostfang bringing his horse’s legs out from under him. The horse had crumpled to the snow, but Zoktavir had risen from it as if nothing had happened, as if this had been how he always planned to dismount, and even the horse had gotten back up, its legs surprisingly unbroken.

name: Name
body:
"It’s been a while, Butcher," Sorscha had said, smiling.
"I know you," he had replied, as though this was new information for both of them.
For a moment, it was the battle she had always imagined. She was faster than him, and Frostfang had danced around his defenses, wearing down his power field, even drawing blood, a freezing slash across his cheek. She felt a savage joy, an exultation she hadn’t felt in years. It was almost too late when she realized the futility of her actions.
The Butcher was taking the blows because he could afford to, and when he struck back, his swing faster than should have been possible, it hit with the force of a thunderclap.
The tide turned in a moment. He was so strong, and Sorscha was far from at her best. Even the blows that she blocked felt like they jarred loose her organs, bruised her bones. She could feel every strike of the axe against Frostfang, all the way down her legs, into her toes. She knew that one direct hit would kill her.
Knowing she was losing ground, she reached out to the magic she could always feel inside her, a cold certainty that curled in her lungs, around her heart. She watched the runes take shape then watched them die as the spell failed—blocked, she realized, by the cursed aura of the axe that was probably about to take her life.

name: Name
body: "You have some strength," the Butcher said with a smile. "I’ll make it quick." A backhand struck her across the face, and she felt bone break, a sharp, wet pop as her vision dimmed and blood poured down her cheek. His boot caught the side of her knee, and she collapsed in the snow. She was blind in one eye, and as she looked up with the other, she saw her father’s killer raising that monstrous axe above her head. She wasn’t sure, even in that moment, whether or not she welcomed its fall. I’m not sure that I deserve to go where you have gone, she told the memory of her lover, but wherever I’m going, I’ll be there soon. The raised axe blocked the weak light of the winter sun, and Sorscha was in shadow. She closed her good eye. "No," said a voice directly in front of her, a shrill voice, shaking with tears. She opened her eye and for a moment couldn’t make sense of what she saw. A figure was standing in the snow, having interposed itself between her and the Butcher, its arms spread wide to make itself as big a target as possible to block the axe’s fall.

name: Name
body: The figure was too small to be a soldier. About the same height as Sorscha where she knelt in the snow, and it was covered in fur. Had Lesnoi conjured some new, strange horror from the woods? But no, almost as quickly as her confusion took root, it was dispelled. Sorscha recognized the voice, the shape, the small, all-too-human hands that stuck out of the ends of the spread arms. "Vlad," she said hoarsely, calling the boy by his given name for the first time. "It’s me you want," the kid said, but he wasn’t speaking to her. He was talking to the Butcher. "I won’t let anyone else die in my place." Sorscha had seen the Butcher at work. Had seen him carve his way through women, children, anything he could reach. And that had been before he joined the Orgoth. Morrow only knew what he was capable of now, and she tried to muster her strength to stand before she felt the spray of warm blood that she knew would be coming any moment. Instead, the big man laughed. "You surprise me, little one," he said. The axe lowered, and the Butcher wrapped his free arm around the young prince’s waist, hoisting him like a babe.

name: Name
body:
Sorscha knew that she had to move. Had to act. She couldn’t see out of her right eye, and blood continued to drip across her face. Pain radiated through every inch of her body, and her bones felt as if they were wrapped in lead, but she managed to lever herself into a standing position with the aid of Frostfang. She didn’t even try to reach out to Bear. She had felt the warjack fall, felt its cortex go out. It was gone. It was just her.
From the Butcher’s arms, the boy looked back toward her. His eyes were rimmed in red, and his cheeks were wet with tears, but for the first time, she saw Vlad in those eyes.
She stumbled forward, using Frostfang like a crutch. Though he had the child in one hand and the massive axe shackled to the other, Zoktavir mounted his horse as if it were nothing. She stumbled toward him, letting momentum keep her on her feet as she drew back Frostfang to strike.
The Butcher pointed at her with his axe, and the ground around her exploded in a conflagration that tore the air from her lungs, sent her sprawling once more to the ground. The last thing she saw was her father’s killer riding away with her lover’s son in his arms. Then darkness closed over her, heavy and quiet and still.

name: Name
body: "You should be happy," Pyotir’s wife said to him anytime he grumbled about his work. "You have the easiest job in the Motherland. Other mechaniks, they have to fix battle damage, they get shot at. You? You dust an old museum piece." It was true that Pyotir had felt a great swelling of pride when he had first been given the assignment. At the time, he had thought of it as a reward for his years of service. Now, he saw it more as a way to quietly shuffle him aside so that younger recruits—ones with less grey in their beards, who didn’t walk with a pronounced limp because of a leg crushed by a falling ’jack—could take his place. Perhaps if Drago had been in an actual museum, it wouldn’t have been so bad. Then, visitors might come by, and Pyotir could tell them about the history and the idiosyncrasies of the famous ’jack who had fought at the side of the Great Prince when he fell at Henge Hold. Likely, that was the eventual fate awaiting the warjack rather than ignominious decommission and salvage, like so many others. For now, however, it wasn’t a priority, so Drago stood, a hulking, silent shadow in a darkened corner of the converted armory at Castle Tzepesci in what had once been a horse stall.

name: Name
body: Pyotir’s job was easy, he had to admit. Certainly the easiest one he’d ever had. And that was part of the problem: He had nothing to do all day. He literally did dust the huge warjack, made sure that its red armor was polished, and checked all of its pistons and gears. Drago was probably in better shape now than it had ever been since the day it had stepped off the factory floor. Every now and then, some higher-up would want to inspect it, and so Pyotir would get it down from its harness and bring it out into the yard with a series of nervous hand gestures that it seemed only grudgingly to obey. Most of the time, however, Drago was a silent companion, as inert as a statue, though it was technically still in service, which meant that part of Pyotir’s duties included keeping it ready for action, so that its boiler could be stoked at a moment’s notice, even if the only action it ever saw was clomping out into the yard to parade in front of one noble or another. What Pyotir mostly did all day was sit at a small wooden table in front of the warjack’s stall, watching the comings and goings of other, more modern soldiers and ’jacks and playing a solitary card game that his grandfather had always called Old Bear.

name: Name
body:
That’s what he was planning to do today, but despite his boredom, Pyotir still took some pride in his work, and he always inspected Drago first thing upon his arrival before he settled in to play cards. There were no gas lamps in the old horse stall, so Pyotir carried his own lantern as he limped back to where the ’jack hung in its harness, thick chains supporting massive leather straps to hold up tons of iron.
Pyotir walked around the warjack, holding the lantern up to examine every familiar dent and ding in its armor. He had a wooden ladder to clean and check the vents on its engine, and he even examined the two mechanika axes that hung on the wall of the stall, noting that one of them could use sharpening again.
He was rubbing at a small spot of dirt or rust on one of the axes when he heard an unmistakable sound behind him, a sound he had trained himself to hear even over the thunder of artillery fire: the faint whoosh of a ’jack’s boiler firing up.
His first thought was to look out into the converted stables that were now part of the castle’s armory. There were other ’jacks out there, but none even remotely close enough that he should have been able to hear them. Which only left . . .

name: Name
body:
Pyotir was in the process of turning as the whoosh became a roar, joined by the screeching of metal as the chains of Drago’s harness tore from the ceiling, one of the massive links striking Pyotir hard enough to send him sprawling into the wall.
The familiar warjack stood now, rather than hanging in the stall. The burning grill that served as its eyes faced Pyotir, and it seemed to breathe heavily, panting. The lamp fell from Pyotir’s nerveless fingers and rolled at his feet, casting canted shadows upon the behemoth above it.
An iron hand reached past Pyotir’s shoulder, close enough that he could feel the heat already beginning to pour off it as the boiler worked overtime. Metal fingers closed around the haft of the axe that Pyotir had just been inspecting.
The mechanik felt the wooden wall behind his back, and he slid down it until he was sitting on the dirt floor of the stall. The ’jack loomed above him, looking even larger from this angle. Pyotir had worked with ’jacks long enough to know that they developed personalities over time, and he was familiar with Drago’s, but he had never seen it in battle, had never seen it like this. He could tell that it wanted to kill him, that it was restraining itself even as it pulled one axe from the wall then the other.

name: Name
body: "Please," Pyotir said, unsure what he was asking of it. Drago’s iron foot came down on the lantern, crushing both casing and fire at once and plunging the stall into a shaky semi-darkness lit only by the glow from the warjack’s boiler. The cries in the rest of the armory began as the heavy ’jack stomped out into the light. The other mechaniks attempted to intervene, shouting orders and gesturing wildly, but Drago simply brushed them aside with the flats of its axes. The repurposed stable was closed by two huge wooden doors, thick enough that it took ’jacks or horses or a half-dozen men to pull them open and closed. Drago splintered them with a sweep of its axes, and then it was gone, leaving a host of soldiers gaping in its wake, Pyotir still sitting in the dirt of the stall staring after it, the cards having spilled from his pocket and scattered on the ground beside him displaying a losing hand. END PART 2
